definition: Natural language generation (NLG) is a software process that produces natural language output.
details: A widely cited survey of NLG methods describes NLG as "the subfield of artificial intelligence and computational linguistics that is concerned with the construction of computer systems that can produce understandable texts in English or other human languages from some underlying non-linguistic representation of information". While it is widely agreed that the output of an NLG process is text, there is disagreement over whether its input must be non-linguistic. Some definitions restrict NLG to generating text from non-linguistic representations. In contemporary NLP, the broader category of text generation may also encompass open-ended generation, summarization, translation, paraphrasing, and question answering. Common applications of NLG methods include the production of various reports, for example weather and patient reports; image captions; and chatbots like ChatGPT. Automated NLG can be compared to the process humans use when they turn ideas into writing or speech. Psycholinguists prefer the term language production for this process, which can also be described in mathematical terms, or modeled in a computer for psychological research. explainer.lead: NLG is the software process that produces natural language output, typically from an underlying non-linguistic representation of information. It matters because it turns structured data into understandable text.

tiers.eli5: It is the step that takes facts stored in a system and writes them out as readable sentences.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use NLG to convert structured information into text. A pitfall is definitional: there is disagreement over whether the input must be non-linguistic, and some definitions restrict NLG to generation from non-linguistic input.
tiers.paperLevel: Defined in a widely cited survey as the subfield of AI and computational linguistics concerned with building systems that produce understandable texts in English or other human languages from some underlying non-linguistic representation of information. It is agreed that output is text; the input requirement is disputed.

explainer.example: A system converts a table of weather measurements into a written forecast sentence.
